newsitem.title: USA: Should you buy the new real bonds?.
newsitem.headline: Should you buy the new real bonds?.

text.p: In a couple of weeks, the Treasury will bestow its belated New Year's present: the so-called "real" bonds that will be indexed to inflation.

Buy one of these babies, and the money you put down is protected against weird occurrences like an OPEC oil embargo or the Hunt brothers buying up silver, or prices shaking off their 15 years of moderation and taking off for the sun.

It could happen: inflation was 13.5 percent in 1980 and probably will reinvigorate itself at some point when everyone has stopped worrying about it altogether. Does that make these inflation-proof bonds, priced for the little guy, a good deal?
Not necessarily.
Because of taxes and the low returns they can expect, investors may end up paying a higher price for the guarantee than it is worth.
The Treasury on Jan. 21 plans to announce the amounts to be auctioned in its first index bond offering. The auction will take place Jan. 29, with trades settling Feb. 6.

You can buy these bonds in many 401(k) plans, through a broker or from the Treasury Department directly, by contacting a local Federal Reserve Bank or writing to the Bureau of the Public Debt, Washington 20239-0001.

The bonds will be sold in denominations as little as $1,000. They'll pay interest that is generally estimated to be around 3 percent a year, and they'll also make good on their inflation-matching claims by adding to your principal every year to make sure it paces the general rate of price changes.

So, if you put $1,000 into one of these bonds this January, and inflation runs 4 percent for the year, your first year's earnings will look like this: $30 interest, payable in two semi-annual instalments, and $40 in inflation-matching interest added to your principal.

That's money you don't see until you cash in the bond. And that's where the tax problems compound. According to John Ziegelbauer, a senior manager in the Washington office of Grant Thornton, a national accounting firm, that interest on principal that you don't see is going to be subject to federal income taxes every year when it is posted to your account.
That means if you are depending on the bonds for current income, you could have years when the income actually received is less than the taxes due on it and the so-called "phantom" income.
How big a problem is that? Possibly not terrible, says Barbara Moore, a senior vice president at SEI Investments in New York, who has done the math.

If you are in the lowest 15 percent tax bracket, inflation would have to reach 19 percent before your tax bill outstripped your annual earnings payout. If you are in the more common 28 percent bracket, that relationship would go against you at an 8.5 percent inflation rate. Those in the 31 percent tax bracket would pay more than they would take in once inflation topped 7.3 percent, and the top 36 percent bracket would suffer at 5 percent inflation.
Clearly they are a better deal for taxpayers in the lower tax brackets.

But, Moore notes, "If inflation does hit that 8 percent level, even if you have to pay out your current taxes, you're going to be very happy you own real bonds." According to Moore, only these inflation-proof bonds will act as real ballast in the event of a stock market meltdown.

Everything else, with the probable exception of real estate, fuels, metals and other commodoties, will slump in a period of high inflation. The principal you hold in traditional bonds will decline when inflation rises as higher interest rates cut the prices on those bonds.
Only "real" bonds will offer real diversification, Moore suggests.
So, do you need or want that diversification?
If you have a long investment horizon and are not the kind of person who looses sleep over her investments, these bonds aren't for you.

But if you are conservative and want to balance the stocks in your portfolio with bonds, this is a better balance than a traditional bond. You might want to put these bonds in a tax-deferred retirement account so you won't have to worry about annual taxes on the principal additions.
Or you may just reason that since these bonds are already exempt from state and local taxes, it's not worth worrying too much about the federal taxes.
After all, once you cash in the bond, all that extra interest will come back to you. You'll have already paid taxes on it, so you won't have to pay them in a big chunk on the bond's sale.
The bottom line? A half-hearted endorsement. These bonds offer protection at a fairly high price. You can do better, but you can surely do worse.
